• Outgoing pipe (18-in, heading south): invert out = ?

Standard practice requires the outgoing invert to be set at or below the LOWEST incoming invert with a 0.10 ft drop for hydraulic continuity. The required outgoing pipe invert elevation is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. The outgoing invert must be 0.10 ft BELOW the lowest incoming invert (74.40), not above it.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! Lowest incoming invert = 74.40 ft. Outgoing = 74.40 − 0.10 = 74.30 ft.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. 74.60 ft is the higher incoming invert. The drop is applied to the LOWEST incoming invert.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Only a 0.10 ft drop is required, not 0.40 ft.

hint:
At a junction manhole, match-line the outgoing pipe to the LOWEST incoming invert, then subtract the required hydraulic drop (typically 0.10 ft).
Lowest incoming = min(74.60, 74.40) = 74.40 ft
Outgoing invert = 74.40 − 0.10 = 74.30 ft
shortcut: Outgoing = min(incoming inverts) − 0.10 = 74.40 − 0.10 = 74.30 ft.
fifthGrader: When two sewers merge into one bigger pipe, the outgoing pipe needs to be slightly lower so gravity keeps pulling the water forward. Engineers call this a 'hydraulic drop'. We just make sure the bottom of the outgoing pipe is a bit lower than the lowest incoming pipe.

title: Profile Sheet – Stationing and Pipe Length
description:
A storm sewer profile sheet shows:

• Manhole A at Station 22+47.50
• Manhole B at Station 26+15.00

The length of pipe between Manhole A and Manhole B is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Convert stations to feet: 26+15.00 = 2615.00 ft, 22+47.50 = 2247.50 ft.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! Station B = 2615.00 ft, Station A = 2247.50 ft. Length = 2615.00 − 2247.50 = 367.50 ft.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Reread the stationing: 22+47.50 means 2247.50 ft, not 2252.50 ft.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Double-check station notation: XX+YY.ZZ means (XX × 100) + YY.ZZ feet.

hint:
Station notation: XX+YY.ZZ = (XX × 100) + YY.ZZ feet.
Station 22+47.50 = 2247.50 ft
Station 26+15.00 = 2615.00 ft
Pipe length = 2615.00 − 2247.50 = 367.50 ft
shortcut: L = 2615.00 − 2247.50 = 367.50 ft. Station math: the '+' means multiply the prefix by 100.
fifthGrader: Stationing is a measuring system used along roads and sewers. The number before the '+' is in hundreds of feet. So 22+47.50 = 2,247.50 feet from the starting point. Subtract to find the distance between two points!

title: Profile Sheet – Hydraulic Grade Line (HGL) Check
description:
A storm sewer profile sheet shows the following at a manhole:

• Pipe crown (top of pipe inside) elevation: 89.60 ft
• Hydraulic Grade Line (HGL) elevation at same manhole: 90.15 ft
• Manhole rim elevation: 92.40 ft

Which statement about flow conditions is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The pipe flows under gravity with free surface flow
options.feedback: Incorrect. The HGL (90.15) is above the pipe crown (89.60), indicating the pipe is pressurized and flows full under pressure.

options.label: B
options.text: The pipe flows full under pressure (surcharged)
options.feedback: Correct! HGL (90.15 ft) > pipe crown (89.60 ft) → pipe is surcharged (flows full under pressure). HGL < rim (92.40 ft) → no surface flooding yet.

options.label: C
options.text: The manhole is actively flooding to the surface
options.feedback: Incorrect. The HGL (90.15) is still below the rim (92.40), so there is no surface flooding.

options.label: D
options.text: The pipe is flowing at critical depth
options.feedback: Incorrect. Critical depth analysis requires Froude number calculation. Here the HGL above the crown is the indicator of pressure flow.

hint:
Three HGL conditions to remember:
• HGL < pipe crown → gravity flow, free surface (partially full)
• HGL > pipe crown but < rim → pipe is surcharged (full, under pressure)
• HGL > rim elevation → active surface flooding
shortcut: HGL = 90.15 > Crown = 89.60 → surcharged. HGL = 90.15 < Rim = 92.40 → no flooding.
fifthGrader: Think of the pipe as a straw. If you blow softly, water trickles along the bottom (free surface). If you blow hard, the straw fills up completely with pressure (surcharged). If you blow REALLY hard, water starts spilling out the top of the manhole (flooding). We compare the HGL to the pipe top and manhole rim to figure out which case we're in.

title: Profile Sheet – Road Vertical Curve Low Point
description:
A road plan-and-profile sheet shows a sag (valley) vertical curve with:

• Incoming grade g1 = -3.0% (descending)
• Outgoing grade g2 = +2.0% (ascending)
• Curve length L = 400 ft
• PVC station: 18+00, PVC elevation: 210.00 ft

The station of the low point on the vertical curve is most nearly:

options.label: B
options.feedback: This is actually the correct answer! Low point x = L × |g1|/(|g1|+|g2|) = 400 × 3/5 = 240 ft from PVC → Station 18+00 + 2+40 = 20+40.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Use x = L × |g1| / (|g1| + |g2|) from PVC.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. The low point is 240 ft past the PVC, not 300 ft.

hint:
For a sag vertical curve, the low point occurs at:
x = L × |g1| / (|g1| + |g2|) from the PVC
x = 400 × 3.0 / (3.0 + 2.0) = 400 × 0.60 = 240 ft
Low point station = 18+00 + 2+40 = 20+40
shortcut: x = 400 × (3/5) = 240 ft from PVC. Low pt = Station 18+00 + 240 ft = 20+40.
fifthGrader: A sag curve is like the bottom of a valley on a road. The lowest point isn't in the middle — it's closer to the steeper incoming grade. We find it by splitting the curve proportionally between the two grades.

title: Profile Sheet – Pipe Invert at Intermediate Point
description:
A sewer profile sheet shows:

• Manhole A at Station 5+00: invert elevation = 82.50 ft
• Manhole B at Station 9+50: invert elevation = 79.05 ft
• The pipe is uniform slope between A and B

The invert elevation of the pipe at Station 7+00 is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Calculate slope first: S = (82.50−79.05)/(950−500) = 3.45/450 = 0.00767. Drop from A to Sta 7+00 = 0.00767 × 200 = 1.53 ft.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Recheck the pipe length: Station 9+50 − 5+00 = 450 ft.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. The drop over 200 ft is 1.53 ft, not 0.75 ft.

hint:
Step 1: Total length = 950 − 500 = 450 ft
Step 2: Slope = (82.50 − 79.05) / 450 = 3.45 / 450 = 0.00767
Step 3: Distance from A to Sta 7+00 = 700 − 500 = 200 ft
Step 4: Drop = 0.00767 × 200 = 1.53 ft
Step 5: Invert at 7+00 = 82.50 − 1.53 = 80.97 ft
fifthGrader: If a pipe drops steadily between two manholes, you can find the elevation at any point in between. Just find the slope (drop per foot), then multiply by the distance from the upstream manhole!

title: Profile Sheet – Freeboard in a Storm Sewer Manhole
description:
A storm sewer profile sheet shows that during the design storm:

• Hydraulic Grade Line (HGL) elevation at Manhole 5: 76.80 ft
• Manhole 5 rim elevation: 79.50 ft

The available freeboard (margin before surface flooding) at Manhole 5 is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Freeboard = Rim elevation − HGL elevation = 79.50 − 76.80.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! Freeboard = 79.50 − 76.80 = 2.70 ft. The system has 2.70 ft of margin before the manhole overflows.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Subtract HGL from rim: 79.50 − 76.80 = 2.70 ft.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Recheck which values are the HGL and which is the rim elevation.

hint: Freeboard = Rim Elevation − Hydraulic Grade Line (HGL) Elevation.
fifthGrader: Freeboard is how much safety margin you have before the water overflows out of the manhole onto the street. The bigger the freeboard, the safer the design. Here, 2.7 ft of freeboard means the water would need to rise 2.7 more feet before street flooding.

title: Profile Sheet – Pipe Crown Elevation
description:
A 36-inch diameter storm sewer profile sheet shows:

• Pipe invert elevation at Station 14+25: 63.40 ft

The pipe crown (top of outside pipe) elevation at Station 14+25 is most nearly (ignore pipe wall thickness):

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Crown = invert + diameter. D = 36 in = 3.0 ft. Crown = 63.40 + 3.0 = 66.40 ft.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. Add the full pipe diameter (3.0 ft), not the radius (1.5 ft).

options.label: C
options.feedback: Correct! D = 36 in = 3.0 ft. Crown = Invert + Diameter = 63.40 + 3.0 = 66.40 ft.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Crown = invert + D = 63.40 + 3.0 = 66.40 ft. You may have used 4.5 ft instead of 3.0 ft.

hint:
Crown elevation = Invert elevation + Pipe Diameter (in feet)
D = 36 inches = 3.0 ft
Crown = 63.40 + 3.0 = 66.40 ft
Note: 'springline' = invert + radius = 63.40 + 1.5 = 64.90 ft
shortcut: Crown = Invert + D = 63.40 + 3.0 = 66.40 ft. Always convert inches to feet first!
fifthGrader: The invert is the bottom of the pipe. The crown is the top. The distance from bottom to top is the pipe diameter. So crown = invert + diameter. Simple addition!

title: Boring Log – Reading SPT N-Value at Depth
description:
A soil boring log shows the following SPT blow count data at a depth of 15 ft:

• 0–6 in (seating): 5 blows
• 6–12 in: 8 blows
• 12–18 in: 11 blows

The uncorrected field SPT N-value to be used for design is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. The seating drive (first 6 inches) is always discarded per ASTM D1586.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. Do NOT include the seating drive. N = 2nd + 3rd increment only.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Correct! N = 8 + 11 = 19 blows/ft. The first 6-inch seating drive (5 blows) is always discarded per ASTM D1586.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. That sums all three increments (5+8+11=24). The seating drive must be excluded.

hint:
ASTM D1586: N = (blows for 6-12 in increment) + (blows for 12-18 in increment)
The first 6-inch increment (0-6 in) is the SEATING DRIVE — always discard it!
N = 8 + 11 = 19 blows/ft
shortcut: N = 2nd + 3rd = 8 + 11 = 19. Never include the 1st 6-inch seating drive.
fifthGrader: Imagine you're hammering a stake into the ground. The first few hits just make contact with the loose stirred-up dirt. Engineers throw away those first hits and only count the next 12 inches of driving. That gives a fair test of the real soil underneath.

title: Boring Log – USCS Soil Classification
description:
A boring log shows the following Atterberg limits and gradation data for a soil sample at 8 ft:

• More than 50% passes the No. 200 sieve (fine-grained soil)
• Liquid Limit (LL) = 38
• Plasticity Index (PI) = 12

Using the USCS Plasticity Chart, the soil classification is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. CH requires LL > 50. Here LL = 38, which is below the 50 threshold.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! Fine-grained, LL < 50 (LL=38), PI = 12. On the plasticity chart, this plots above the A-line (A-line PI = 0.73(LL−20) = 0.73×18 = 13.1 ≈ close but below → CL). Classified as CL — Lean Clay.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. ML plots below the A-line on the plasticity chart. Check: A-line PI at LL=38 is 0.73(38−20) = 13.1. PI=12 is just below the A-line → ML is possible. This is a borderline case, but CL is the more common answer for LL≈38, PI=12.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. MH requires LL > 50.

hint:
USCS for fine-grained soils (>50% passes #200):
Step 1: If LL < 50 → Low plasticity (first letter L)
Step 2: A-line equation: PI = 0.73 × (LL − 20)
At LL=38: A-line PI = 0.73 × 18 = 13.1
• If PI > A-line → Clay (C): CL (LL<50) or CH (LL>50)
• If PI < A-line → Silt (M): ML (LL<50) or MH (LL>50)
shortcut: A-line PI at LL=38 = 0.73×(38−20) = 13.1. Actual PI = 12 < 13.1 → slightly below A-line → ML/CL boundary.
fifthGrader: The Plasticity Chart is like a map that tells you if soil is more like clay (sticky) or silt (silty). Clay is above the A-line on the chart. Silt is below. The LL tells you how wet the soil can get before it flows, and PI tells you its range of plasticity.

title: Boring Log – Water Table Depth
description:
A boring log shows the following observations:

• Ground surface elevation: 124.50 ft
• Water table encountered at 8.5 ft below ground surface
• Boring terminated at 30 ft depth

The groundwater table (GWT) elevation is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. GWT = Ground Surface − depth to water = 124.50 − 8.5 = 116.0 ft.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! GWT elevation = 124.50 − 8.5 = 116.00 ft.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. The depth to water is 8.5 ft, not 5.0 ft. Recheck: 124.50 − 8.5 = 116.0 ft.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Subtract depth to water from ground surface — do not add.

hint: GWT elevation = Ground surface elevation − Depth to water table = 124.50 − 8.5 = 116.00 ft.
shortcut: GWT = 124.50 − 8.50 = 116.00 ft. Depth below ground always subtracts from ground elevation.
fifthGrader: The boring log shows how deep they drilled and what they found. When they hit water, they note the depth. To get the water's elevation, just subtract that depth from the ground surface elevation — like going down 8.5 floors in a building!

title: Boring Log – AASHTO Soil Classification
description:
A roadway subgrade boring log shows:

• Percent passing No. 200 sieve = 42%
• Percent passing No. 40 sieve = 68%
• Liquid Limit (LL) = 29
• Plasticity Index (PI) = 8

Using the AASHTO classification system, this soil is most nearly classified as:

options.label: A
options.text: A-2-4 (Silty or Clayey Gravel and Sand)
options.feedback: Incorrect. A-2 requires less than 35% passing the No. 200 sieve. Here 42% passes, so this is a silt-clay material.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! >35% passes No. 200 → silt-clay material. LL ≤ 40 and PI ≤ 10 → A-4 (Silty soil). A-4 is a poor subgrade material.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. A-6 requires PI > 10. Here PI = 8, which falls in the A-4 range (LL ≤ 40, PI ≤ 10).

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. A-7 requires LL > 40. Here LL = 29, which is below the threshold.

hint:
AASHTO Classification steps:
Step 1: >35% passes No. 200 → Silt-Clay Materials (A-4 through A-7)
Step 2: Check LL and PI:
• A-4: LL ≤ 40, PI ≤ 10
• A-5: LL > 40, PI ≤ 10
• A-6: LL ≤ 40, PI > 10
• A-7: LL > 40, PI > 10
LL = 29 (≤40), PI = 8 (≤10) → A-4
fifthGrader: AASHTO is a grading system for road soils — like report cards. A-1 is the best (gravels and sands, great for roads). A-4 through A-7 are the worst (fine silts and clays that swell when wet). This soil is A-4, a poor-quality subgrade that needs special treatment.

title: Boring Log – Relative Density from N-Value
description: A boring log shows a corrected SPT N-value of (N1)60 = 28 blows/ft in a clean sand deposit. Based on the standard Terzaghi & Peck relative density correlation table, the relative density and density description are most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Very Loose corresponds to (N1)60 < 4. N=28 is much higher.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. Medium Dense is (N1)60 = 10–30. N=28 is at the upper end of Medium Dense, but the standard ranges push it into Dense.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Correct! (N1)60 = 28 falls in the Dense range (30–50 blows/ft per most references). Standard table: 0–4 Very Loose, 4–10 Loose, 10–30 Medium, 30–50 Dense, >50 Very Dense.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Very Dense corresponds to (N1)60 > 50. N=28 is not that high.

hint:
Standard SPT Relative Density Correlation (clean sand):
• (N1)60 = 0–4: Very Loose
• (N1)60 = 4–10: Loose
• (N1)60 = 10–30: Medium Dense
• (N1)60 = 30–50: Dense
• (N1)60 > 50: Very Dense
shortcut: (N1)60 = 28 → upper end of Medium Dense (10-30 range). Many references classify 28 as Dense (30-50). Know your reference handbook table.
fifthGrader: The SPT blow count is like a hardness test for soil. If it's easy to hammer a pipe into the ground (few blows), the soil is loose. If it's hard to hammer it in (many blows), the soil is dense and strong. 28 blows is pretty hard — that's Dense sand!

title: Boring Log – Effective Overburden Stress Calculation
description:
A boring log and soil profile show:

• 0 to 5 ft: Dry sand, total unit weight γ = 115 pcf
• 5 to 12 ft: Saturated clay, γsat = 122 pcf
• Groundwater table at 5 ft depth
• γw = 62.4 pcf

The effective vertical stress σ'v at 12 ft depth is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Remember to use buoyant unit weight below GWT: γ' = γsat − γw = 122 − 62.4 = 59.6 pcf.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. You used total stress below GWT instead of effective stress (buoyant weight).

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Do not add pore water pressure to total stress — subtract it to get effective stress.

hint:
Effective stress = Total vertical stress − Pore water pressure
Above GWT: σ'v = γ_dry × depth
Below GWT: use buoyant unit weight γ' = γsat − γw
σ'v = (5 × 115) + (7 × (122 − 62.4)) = 575 + 417.2 = 992 psf
shortcut: σ'v = 5×115 + 7×(122−62.4) = 575 + 417 = 992 psf. Buoyant weight = γsat − γw below GWT.
fifthGrader: Underwater, things feel lighter because water pushes up (buoyancy). Soil below the water table is also 'lighter' in the same way. We subtract the water's weight from the soil's weight to get the effective stress — the stress that actually squeezes soil particles together.

title: Boring Log – Layer Identification from Blow Count Trend
description:
A boring log shows the following SPT N-values with depth:

• 5 ft: N = 3
• 10 ft: N = 4
• 15 ft: N = 6
• 20 ft: N = 2  ← sudden drop
• 25 ft: N = 3
• 30 ft: N = 18
• 35 ft: N = 28

The sudden drop in N-value at 20 ft most likely indicates:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Dense gravel would cause N to increase sharply, not decrease.

options.label: B
options.text: A soft clay or organic layer
options.feedback: Correct! A sudden drop in N-value (from 6 to 2) indicates a weak layer — likely soft clay, loose silt, or organic material. This is a critical geotechnical finding.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Bedrock causes N to increase to very high values (50+), often recorded as 'refusal'.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sudden drops are geotechnically meaningful — they indicate weak layers and should never be dismissed as errors.

hint:
N-value trend interpretation:
• Increasing N with depth → normal consolidation, increasing density
• Very high N (>50 or refusal) → dense gravel, cemented soil, or bedrock
• Sudden DROP in N → weak layer: soft clay, loose sand, or organic soil
• Very low N (1-3) → potentially liquefiable sand or compressible clay
shortcut: N drops from 6 to 2 at 20 ft → soft/weak layer. Watch for sudden N drops — they identify problem soils.
fifthGrader: The blow count is like a hardness test. If the soil suddenly becomes easy to hammer into (low blow count), you've hit a weak spot — like hitting pudding after digging through dirt. Engineers look for these weak spots because they can cause buildings to settle unevenly.

title: Boring Log – Liquefaction Susceptibility
description: A boring log shows a loose, saturated, clean fine sand layer at 18 ft depth with corrected SPT value (N1)60 = 12 blows/ft. The cyclic resistance ratio (CRR) from the standard Seed & Idriss chart at (N1)60 = 12 is approximately 0.14. The cyclic stress ratio (CSR) for the design earthquake is 0.18. The factor of safety against liquefaction is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. FS = CRR / CSR = 0.14 / 0.18. Recheck your division.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! FS = CRR / CSR = 0.14 / 0.18 = 0.78. Since FS < 1.0, liquefaction is likely during the design earthquake.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. You may have inverted the ratio. FS = CRR/CSR, not CSR/CRR.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. FS = 0.14/0.18 = 0.78 < 1.0, indicating liquefaction is expected.

hint:
Factor of Safety against liquefaction:
FS = CRR / CSR
• FS < 1.0 → Liquefaction likely
• FS ≥ 1.0 → Liquefaction unlikely
FS = 0.14 / 0.18 = 0.78 < 1.0 → Liquefaction likely
shortcut: FS = CRR/CSR = 0.14/0.18 = 0.78 < 1.0 → LIQUEFACTION LIKELY. The soil cannot resist the earthquake shaking.
fifthGrader: Liquefaction is when an earthquake shakes loose wet sand so violently that it acts like quicksand. The CRR is how much shaking the sand can resist. The CSR is how much shaking the earthquake actually causes. If the earthquake shakes harder than the sand can handle (FS < 1), the sand liquefies!

title: Boring Log – Sample Recovery and RQD
description:
A rock core boring log shows the following for a 5-ft core run:

• Total core recovered: 4.20 ft
• Pieces of intact core ≥ 4 inches long: 2.80 ft total

The Rock Quality Designation (RQD) for this core run is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Correct! RQD = (sum of pieces ≥ 4 in) / (total core run length) × 100 = 2.80 / 5.00 × 100 = 56%.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. RQD uses the TOTAL core run length (5.0 ft) in the denominator, not the recovered length (4.2 ft).

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. RQD is based on pieces ≥ 4 inches long (2.80 ft), not total recovery (4.20 ft).

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. RQD = 100% only if all recovered core is in pieces ≥ 4 inches long.

hint:
RQD = Σ(intact pieces ≥ 4 inches) / Total Core Run Length × 100%
Denominator = total length drilled (5.0 ft), NOT recovered length
RQD = 2.80 / 5.00 × 100 = 56%
RQD scale: 0-25% Very Poor, 25-50% Poor, 50-75% Fair, 75-90% Good, 90-100% Excellent
shortcut: RQD = 2.80/5.00 × 100 = 56%. Always divide by TOTAL drill run, not recovered core.
fifthGrader: RQD measures how 'together' a rock is. If the rock drills out in big solid pieces (4 inches or longer), it's good quality. If it crumbles into tiny bits, it's poor quality. We add up only the big solid pieces and divide by how far we drilled — like measuring how many good eggs you got out of a whole carton.

title: Boring Log – Consolidation Layer Identification
description:
A boring log shows a 6-ft thick soft clay layer (N = 2 to 4) sandwiched between sand layers. Laboratory testing shows:

• Initial void ratio e0 = 1.20
• Compression index Cc = 0.42
• Initial effective stress σ'v0 = 800 psf
• Added stress Δσ = 400 psf

The primary consolidation settlement of the clay layer is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Use: S = (Cc × H / (1+e0)) × log10((σ'v0 + Δσ) / σ'v0).

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Check your H conversion (H = 6 ft = 72 in) and your log10 calculation.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is too large. Recheck Cc = 0.42, e0 = 1.20, and the stress ratio log10(1200/800) = 0.176.

fifthGrader: Clay is like a sponge. When you put a load on it, water slowly squeezes out and the clay shrinks. The Compression Index Cc tells you how squishy the clay is. The settlement equation tells you exactly how much the layer shrinks under the new building load.

title: Earthwork – Average End Area Method
description:
A road construction project has the following cross-section data:

• Station 10+00: Cut area = 125 ft²
• Station 11+00: Cut area = 190 ft²

Using the Average End Area method, the volume of cut between the two stations is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. V = [(A1+A2)/2] × L. Then convert ft³ to yd³ by dividing by 27.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Use the average of the two end areas, not the sum.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. You may have forgotten to divide by 2 when averaging, or forgot to convert ft³ to yd³.

hint:
Average End Area Method: V = [(A1 + A2) / 2] × L
V = [(125 + 190) / 2] × 100 ft = 157.5 × 100 = 15,750 ft³
Convert to cubic yards: 15,750 / 27 = 583 yd³
Note: 1 yd³ = 27 ft³
fifthGrader: Imagine slicing a loaf of bread. Each slice is a cross-section. To find the volume of bread between two slices, average their areas and multiply by the distance between them. Then convert from cubic feet to cubic yards (27 cubic feet = 1 cubic yard).

title: Earthwork – Prismoidal Formula
description:
Using the Prismoidal Formula, calculate the volume of a roadway embankment between two stations:

• Station 15+00: Fill area A1 = 80 ft²
• Midpoint area Am = 110 ft² (field measured)
• Station 16+00: Fill area A2 = 140 ft²
• Length L = 100 ft

The volume using the Prismoidal Formula is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Prismoidal formula: V = (L/6) × (A1 + 4Am + A2). Don't forget the factor of 4 for the midpoint area.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. You may have used the Average End Area method. The prismoidal formula weights the middle section (4×Am) more heavily.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Recheck the formula: V = (L/6)(A1 + 4Am + A2). Note L/6, not L/3.

shortcut: V = (L/6)(A1 + 4Am + A2) = (100/6)(660) = 11,000 ft³ / 27 = 407 yd³. More accurate than end-area method.
fifthGrader: The prismoidal formula is the 'upgraded' version of the average end area method. Instead of just averaging the two ends, it also measures the middle of the section. The middle gets 4 times more weight because it best represents the actual shape.

title: Earthwork – Shrinkage and Swell Factors
description: A cut section produces 10,000 bank cubic yards (BCY) of clay. The clay has a swell factor of 30% (it expands when excavated). It will be used as fill material with a shrinkage factor of 15% (it compacts when placed). The volume of compacted fill (CY) this cut will produce is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. To convert BCY to compacted CY: Compacted CY = BCY × (1 − shrinkage) = 10,000 × 0.85 = 8,500 CY.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! Compacted CY = BCY × (1 − shrinkage factor) = 10,000 × (1 − 0.15) = 10,000 × 0.85 = 8,500 CY.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. That would be loose (truck) volume, not compacted volume.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. That uses the swell factor. For compacted fill volume, use: BCY × (1 − shrinkage).

hint:
Volume Conversion:
• Loose (truck) volume = BCY × (1 + swell factor)
• Compacted fill volume = BCY × (1 − shrinkage factor)
Compacted CY = 10,000 × (1 − 0.15) = 8,500 CY
shortcut: Compacted CY = BCY × (1 − shrinkage) = 10,000 × 0.85 = 8,500 CY. Swell is for truck loads, not final fill.
fifthGrader: When you dig up dirt (bank), it fluffs up like popcorn (swell — good for counting trucks). But when you put it back down and compact it, it squishes smaller than it was originally. That squishing is the shrinkage factor. 15% shrinkage means you get only 85% of the bank volume back as compacted fill.

title: Earthwork – Mass Diagram Balance Point
description:
A highway mass diagram shows accumulated earthwork (in yd³) from left to right. A balance line drawn on the mass diagram intersects the curve at two points:

• Left intersection at Station 12+00
• Right intersection at Station 18+00

The free haul distance allowed in the contract is 500 ft. The overhaul distance (requiring extra payment) is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Total haul = distance between balance points = 600 ft. Overhaul = 600 − 500 = 100 ft.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! Distance between balance points = Station 18+00 − 12+00 = 600 ft. Overhaul = 600 − 500 (free haul) = 100 ft.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. 500 ft is the free haul distance, not the overhaul distance.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. 600 ft is the total haul distance. Overhaul = total − free haul = 600 − 500 = 100 ft.

hint:
Total haul distance = distance between the two balance line intersections
= 1800 − 1200 = 600 ft
Overhaul distance = Total haul − Free haul distance
= 600 − 500 = 100 ft
fifthGrader: Moving dirt costs money — especially if you have to haul it far. The 'free haul' is the distance you can move dirt for free (included in the base price). Anything beyond that (the 'overhaul') costs extra because it's farther than expected.

title: Earthwork – Borrow Volume Calculation
description: A project requires 5,000 bank cubic yards (BCY) of fill material. After computing cut and fill from the road profile, a deficit of 2,000 BCY exists. The remaining 2,000 BCY must be borrowed from an offsite borrow pit. The soil has a swell factor of 25%. The volume of loose material (LCY) that must be loaded and hauled from the borrow pit is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. The borrow pit provides BCY. To find truck volume (LCY), multiply BCY × (1 + swell).

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. 2,000 BCY ≠ 2,000 LCY. The loose volume is larger than the bank volume by the swell factor.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. 2,000 × 1.25 = 2,500 LCY. You may have used a swell factor of 50%.

hint:
Loose (truck) volume = Bank volume × (1 + swell factor)
LCY = 2,000 BCY × 1.25 = 2,500 LCY
This is the volume loaded onto trucks at the borrow pit.
shortcut: LCY = BCY × (1 + swell) = 2,000 × 1.25 = 2,500 LCY. Dirt expands when you dig it up!
fifthGrader: Dirt is like popcorn — compact in the ground (bank), but fluffy when you dig it up and put it in a truck (loose). The swell factor tells you how much it fluffs. 25% swell means every 100 truckloads becomes 125 truckloads worth of loose dirt. So 2,000 bank yards becomes 2,500 truckload yards.

title: Earthwork – Grid Method Volume
description:
A rectangular site 100 ft × 60 ft is divided into a 4 × 3 grid of equal cells (10 ft × 20 ft each). The existing grade and proposed grade differ at each grid point. The sum of all cut heights at grid corners is as follows:

• Corner points (appear in 1 cell): Σh = 8.0 ft (4 corners × 2.0 ft avg)
• Edge points (appear in 2 cells): Σh = 12.0 ft
• Interior points (appear in 4 cells): Σh = 6.0 ft

Using the grid volume formula V = (A_cell/4) × (Σh1 + 2Σh2 + 4Σh4), the total cut volume is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Use V = (A_cell/4)(Σh_corner + 2Σh_edge + 4Σh_interior). A_cell = 10×20 = 200 ft².

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Check your weighting factors: corners ×1, edges ×2, interior ×4.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. You may have forgotten to divide by 4 in the A_cell/4 term.

hint:
Grid method: V = (A_cell / 4) × (Σh1 + 2×Σh2 + 4×Σh4)
where h1 = corner points, h2 = edge points, h4 = interior points
A_cell = 10 × 20 = 200 ft²
V = (200/4) × (8.0 + 2×12.0 + 4×6.0) = 50 × 56 = 2,800 ft³
shortcut: V = 50 × (8 + 24 + 24) = 50 × 56 = 2,800 ft³. Interior points get weight 4, edges weight 2, corners weight 1.
fifthGrader: The grid method divides a site into little squares. At each corner of each square, you measure how deep to cut. Corner points only belong to one square (weight 1). Edge points are shared by 2 squares (weight 2). Interior points are shared by 4 squares (weight 4). Add it all up and you get the volume!

title: Earthwork – Cut/Fill Balance Station
description:
A road profile shows:

• From Station 0+00 to 8+00: Cut section, total cut = 800 BCY
• From Station 8+00 to 14+00: Fill section, required fill = 800 BCY
• The cut material has a 10% shrinkage factor

Is the project in balance (cut = fill required), considering shrinkage?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — the project is balanced at 800 yd³ each
options.feedback: Incorrect. The cut provides 800 BCY, but after 10% shrinkage it only compacts to 800 × 0.90 = 720 CY. Fill requires 800 CY.

options.label: B
options.text: No — there is a deficit of 80 yd³ of compacted fill
options.feedback: Correct! Cut of 800 BCY × (1 − 0.10) = 720 compacted CY. Fill required = 800 CY. Deficit = 800 − 720 = 80 CY of compacted fill.

options.label: C
options.text: No — there is a surplus of 80 yd³ of cut material
options.feedback: Incorrect. Shrinkage creates a DEFICIT, not a surplus. The cut material shrinks when compacted.

options.label: D
options.text: No — there is a deficit of 800 yd³
options.feedback: Incorrect. Recheck: deficit = 800 − 720 = 80 CY, not 800 CY.

hint:
Compacted fill from cut = BCY × (1 − shrinkage) = 800 × 0.90 = 720 CY
Fill required = 800 CY
Deficit = 800 − 720 = 80 CY
Shrinkage always creates a fill deficit — you need borrow material to make up the difference.
shortcut: Compacted yield = 800 × 0.90 = 720 CY < 800 CY needed → deficit of 80 CY.
fifthGrader: When you dig up 800 yards of dirt and try to put it back compacted, it squishes down. With 10% shrinkage, your 800 yards of fluffy dirt becomes only 720 yards when packed tight. So you're short 80 yards — you need to get more dirt from somewhere else!

title: Earthwork – Truck Load Count
description: An excavation produces 3,600 bank cubic yards (BCY) of soil with a swell factor of 20%. Each dump truck carries 12 loose cubic yards (LCY) per load. The total number of truck loads required to haul away all excavated material is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. First convert BCY to LCY: LCY = BCY × (1 + swell) = 3600 × 1.20 = 4,320 LCY.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. You forgot to account for swell. The loose volume is larger than the bank volume.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. LCY = 3600 × 1.20 = 4,320. Loads = 4,320 / 12 = 360. Round up any fractional loads.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Correct! LCY = 3,600 × 1.20 = 4,320 LCY. Loads = 4,320 / 12 = 360 loads.

hint:
Step 1: Convert BCY to LCY: LCY = BCY × (1 + swell) = 3,600 × 1.20 = 4,320 LCY
Step 2: Loads = LCY / truck capacity = 4,320 / 12 = 360 loads
Always round UP (partial loads still require a truck trip).
fifthGrader: Dirt fluffs up when you dig it. So 3,600 yards of packed-in-the-ground dirt becomes 4,320 yards of fluffy truck-load dirt. Divide by 12 yards per truck and you need 360 trips!

title: Earthwork – Contour Area Method
description:
A topographic map shows a pond to be excavated. Contour areas at each elevation are:

• El. 100 ft (bottom): A = 0 ft²
• El. 102 ft: A = 4,200 ft²
• El. 104 ft: A = 9,800 ft²
• El. 106 ft (top): A = 16,500 ft²

Using the Average End Area method between each 2-ft contour interval, the total volume of excavation is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sum the volumes between each contour pair using Average End Area.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Sum three separate Average End Area volumes, one per contour interval.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Do not sum all areas and multiply by total depth.

fifthGrader: This is like stacking a bunch of pancakes of different sizes to figure out how much batter you used. Each 2-foot layer between contour lines is a 'pancake', and you average the top and bottom to find each layer's volume. Add all the pancake volumes together for the total!

title: Earthwork – Pay Volume vs. Neat Line
description:
A trench excavation drawing shows:

• Trench depth: 6 ft
• Neat line (minimum pay) width: 3 ft
• Actual excavated width: 4.5 ft (over-excavated)
• Trench length: 200 ft

The contractor is paid for the neat line volume only. The pay quantity for excavation is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Correct! Pay volume = Neat line dimensions only: V = 3 × 6 × 200 = 3,600 ft³. 3,600 / 27 = 133 yd³.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. The contractor is paid for the NEAT LINE volume (3 ft × 6 ft × 200 ft), not the actual excavated volume.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. That uses the actual width of 4.5 ft. Pay volume is based on neat line (3 ft) only.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. This is far too large. Check your dimensions and unit conversion.

hint:
Pay volume uses NEAT LINE dimensions (the minimum required opening), regardless of actual over-excavation.
V_pay = Width_neat × Depth × Length = 3 × 6 × 200 = 3,600 ft³
Convert: 3,600 / 27 = 133 yd³
shortcut: V = 3 × 6 × 200 = 3,600 ft³ / 27 = 133 yd³. Over-excavation is at the contractor's expense.
fifthGrader: When a contractor digs a trench wider than specified, they don't get paid extra for the extra dirt. The plans show the minimum width needed (neat line), and that's the width used for payment. Digging too wide is the contractor's mistake and cost.

title: Structural Detail – Rebar Designation and Area
description: A concrete beam detail shows 4-#8 bars in the tension zone. The nominal diameter of a #8 rebar is 1.0 inch. The total steel area As provided is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Area per #8 bar = π(1.0)²/4 = 0.785 in². Total = 4 × 0.785 = 3.14 in².

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! Area per bar = π × (1.0)²/4 = 0.785 in². Total As = 4 × 0.785 = 3.14 in².

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. The area is not 1.0 in² per bar. A = π/4 × d² = π/4 × 1.0² = 0.785 in².

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. That is 4 × #9 bars. For #8 bars, d = 1.0 in, A_bar = 0.785 in².

hint:
Rebar designation: #N bar has nominal diameter = N/8 inches
• #8 bar: d = 8/8 = 1.0 inch
• Area per bar: A = π × d² / 4 = π × 1.0² / 4 = 0.785 in²
• Total As = 4 × 0.785 = 3.14 in²
shortcut: Rebar area table: #8 = 0.79 in²/bar. As = 4 × 0.79 = 3.16 ≈ 3.14 in². Memorize common bar areas for the PE exam.
fifthGrader: Rebar bars are named by their size in eighths of an inch. A #8 bar is 8 eighths = 1 inch in diameter. To find the area of a circle, use π × r² or π × d²/4. Four bars together have 4 times the area of one bar.

title: Structural Detail – Minimum Concrete Cover
description:
A concrete column detail for an outdoor exposed structure shows:

• Main vertical bars: #8 bars
• Ties: #4 bars at 12 in spacing
• ACI minimum cover for cast-in-place concrete exposed to weather: 1.5 in for #5 and smaller, 2.0 in for #6 and larger

The minimum concrete cover requirement for the #8 main bars is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. 0.75 in is the minimum for protected slabs, not exposed columns.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. 1.5 in applies to bars #5 and smaller. The #8 bar is larger than #5.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Correct! Per ACI 318, for concrete exposed to weather: bars #6 and larger require 2.0 inches of cover. #8 > #6, so minimum cover = 2.0 in.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. 3.0 in is the minimum for cast-in-place concrete in contact with ground (not just exposed to weather).

hint:
ACI 318 Minimum Cover for Concrete Exposed to Weather:
• #6, #7, #8 bars and larger: 2 inches
• #5 bars and smaller (≤ 5/8 in dia): 1.5 inches
• Cast against/permanently in contact with ground: 3 inches
shortcut: If bar # ≥ 6 and exposed to weather → cover = 2.0 in. If bar ≤ 5 → 1.5 in.
fifthGrader: Concrete cover protects steel from rusting. Outdoor concrete needs more cover because rain and moisture can seep in and corrode the steel. Bigger bars get more cover because they carry more load and rust is more dangerous. Think of it as a thicker raincoat for bigger bars.

title: Structural Detail – Bolt Pattern Spacing Check
description:
A steel connection detail shows 3/4-inch diameter A325 bolts in a row. AISC requirements specify:
• Minimum bolt spacing: 2-2/3 × bolt diameter
• Standard recommended spacing: 3 × bolt diameter

The minimum acceptable center-to-center bolt spacing is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Minimum spacing = 2-2/3 × d = 2.667 × 0.75 = 2.0 in (not 1.5 in).

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! Minimum spacing = 2-2/3 × d = (8/3) × 0.75 = 2.0 in.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. 2.25 in = 3 × 0.75, which is the PREFERRED spacing, not the minimum.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. 3.0 in would apply to a 1-inch bolt. For 3/4-in bolt, preferred = 3 × 0.75 = 2.25 in.

hint:
AISC minimum bolt spacing = 2-2/3 × bolt diameter = (8/3) × d
For 3/4-in bolts: min spacing = (8/3) × 0.75 = 2.0 in
Preferred/standard spacing = 3 × d = 3 × 0.75 = 2.25 in
fifthGrader: Bolts in steel connections need to be spread out enough so the steel between them doesn't tear. The rule says they need at least 2-2/3 times their own diameter of space. For a 3/4-inch bolt, that's about 2 inches between bolt centers.

title: Structural Detail – Weld Size from Drawing
description: A structural detail shows a fillet weld symbol with the number '5/16' on the left side of the weld symbol. The base metal is 3/8-inch thick A36 steel plate. The specified weld size is 5/16 inch. Checking AISC minimum fillet weld size (based on thicker plate joined), the minimum required weld size for 3/8-in plate is:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. AISC min for plates > 1/4 in to 1/2 in thick is 3/16 in. 5/16 > 3/16 → acceptable, but identify the correct minimum.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! AISC Table J2.4: For thicker plate 3/8 in (which is > 1/4 in but ≤ 1/2 in), minimum fillet weld = 3/16 in. Specified 5/16 in > 3/16 in → weld is acceptable.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. The minimum is 3/16 in for this plate thickness. The specified 5/16 in weld exceeds the minimum.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. The AISC minimum for a 3/8-in plate is 3/16 in, not 5/16 in.

hint:
AISC Minimum Fillet Weld Size (Table J2.4) — based on thicker part joined:
• Plate ≤ 1/4 in thick: min weld = 1/8 in
• 1/4 in < plate ≤ 1/2 in: min weld = 3/16 in
• 1/2 in < plate ≤ 3/4 in: min weld = 1/4 in
• Plate > 3/4 in: min weld = 5/16 in
For 3/8-in plate: min = 3/16 in. Specified 5/16 in > 3/16 in ✓
shortcut: 3/8-in plate falls in the (1/4–1/2 in] range → min weld = 3/16 in. Specified 5/16 in > 3/16 in → OK.
fifthGrader: A fillet weld is a triangle of metal connecting two pieces of steel. The number on the drawing tells you how big that triangle is. Engineers have to check that the weld is big enough for the thickness of the metal being joined — thin metal gets a small minimum weld, thick metal gets a bigger minimum weld.

title: Structural Detail – Beam Effective Depth
description:
A reinforced concrete beam detail shows:

• Total beam depth h = 24 inches
• Bottom steel: 3-#9 bars (one layer)
• Stirrups: #3 bars
• Clear cover to stirrups: 1.5 inches

The effective depth d (from compression face to centroid of tension steel) is most nearly:
(Use: d = h − cover − stirrup dia − half of main bar dia)
#9 bar diameter = 1.128 in, #3 bar diameter = 0.375 in

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. d = h − cover − d_stirrup − (d_bar/2) = 24 − 1.5 − 0.375 − 0.564 = 21.56 in.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Don't forget to subtract the stirrup diameter and half the main bar diameter.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. You may have used half the cover or forgotten the stirrup diameter.

hint:
Effective depth: d = h − (clear cover) − (stirrup diameter) − (half main bar diameter)
d = 24 − 1.5 − 0.375 − (1.128/2)
d = 24 − 1.5 − 0.375 − 0.564 = 21.56 in
shortcut: d = 24 − 1.5 − 0.375 − 0.564 = 21.56 in ≈ 21.6 in. Always measure to the CENTROID of the steel.
fifthGrader: Effective depth is the distance from the top of the beam down to the center of the steel bars. The concrete above the steel is what resists the compression (squeezing). More effective depth = the beam can carry more load. We have to subtract the cover, the stirrup size, and half the bar diameter to find the center of the steel.

title: Structural Detail – Column Tie Spacing
description:
A concrete column detail shows 8-#10 longitudinal bars with #4 tie bars. Per ACI 318, the maximum tie spacing is the smallest of:
• 16 × longitudinal bar diameter
• 48 × tie bar diameter
• Least column dimension

The column is 18 in × 18 in square. #10 bar d = 1.27 in, #4 bar d = 0.50 in. The maximum allowable tie spacing is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Compare all three criteria and select the MINIMUM: 16×1.27=20.3 in, 48×0.50=24 in, column=18 in.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. 20.3 in is one criterion but not the minimum. Check: 18 in < 20.3 in.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Correct! Criteria: (1) 16 × 1.27 = 20.3 in, (2) 48 × 0.50 = 24.0 in, (3) 18 in (column dimension). Minimum = 18 in → maximum tie spacing = 18 in.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. 24 in is the largest of the three criteria. The SMALLEST governs for maximum tie spacing.

hint:
ACI 318 Max Tie Spacing — use the MINIMUM of:
① 16 × d_longitudinal = 16 × 1.27 = 20.3 in
② 48 × d_tie = 48 × 0.50 = 24.0 in
③ Least column dimension = 18 in
Min (20.3, 24.0, 18.0) = 18.0 in → Maximum tie spacing = 18 in
shortcut: min(16×1.27, 48×0.50, 18) = min(20.3, 24, 18) = 18 in. Column dimension governs.
fifthGrader: Column ties are like rings around the main bars, keeping them from buckling outward. ACI gives three rules for how far apart these rings can be — you must follow all three and use the smallest answer. Here the column width (18 in) is the tightest restriction, so it controls.

title: Structural Detail – Steel Section Properties from Table
description:
A structural drawing specifies a W18×97 wide-flange steel section. From the AISC Steel Construction Manual (or NCEES Reference Handbook), a W18×97 has:

• Ix = 1,750 in⁴ (strong axis moment of inertia)
• d = 18.6 in (total depth)

The elastic section modulus Sx about the strong axis is most nearly:

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Use c = d/2 = 9.3 in. Sx = 1750/9.3 = 188 in³, not 1750/8.3.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. You may have multiplied instead of divided. Sx = Ix / c, not Ix × c.

hint:
Elastic section modulus: Sx = Ix / c
where c = distance from neutral axis to extreme fiber = d/2 for symmetric sections
c = 18.6 / 2 = 9.3 in
Sx = 1,750 / 9.3 = 188 in³
shortcut: Sx = Ix / (d/2) = 1750 / 9.3 = 188 in³. Also readable directly from AISC tables.
fifthGrader: The section modulus tells engineers how resistant a beam is to bending stress. A deeper beam (larger d) or one with more area far from the center (larger I) handles bending better. We calculate Sx by dividing I by the distance from the center to the edge.

title: Structural Detail – Slab Reinforcement Spacing
description:
A one-way concrete slab detail shows:

• Slab thickness h = 6 inches
• Required As = 0.24 in²/ft of width
• Available bars: #4 bars (Ab = 0.20 in²/bar)

The required bar spacing to provide As = 0.24 in²/ft is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Spacing = (Ab / As_required) × 12 = (0.20/0.24) × 12 = 10 in.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. At s = 12 in, As = 0.20 in²/ft < 0.24 required. Bars must be closer together.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. At larger spacing you provide LESS steel, not more. Increase spacing only if bars are larger.

hint:
Slab bar spacing: s = (Ab / As_required) × 12 in/ft
s = (0.20 in²/bar) / (0.24 in²/ft) × 12 in/ft
s = 0.833 × 12 = 10 in on center
shortcut: s = (Ab/As) × 12 = (0.20/0.24) × 12 = 10 in o.c. Smaller spacing = more steel per foot.
fifthGrader: Imagine evenly spacing fence posts across a yard. If each post (bar) is a certain size (Ab), and you need a total coverage (As) per foot, you calculate how far apart to place the posts. Closer posts = more coverage. Here, 10 inches apart gives exactly enough steel per foot.

title: Structural Detail – Development Length
description:
A beam-column connection detail requires a #8 straight bar to be developed in tension. f'c = 4,000 psi, fy = 60,000 psi, normal weight concrete, uncoated bar, more than 12 in of concrete below bar. Using the ACI 318 simplified formula:

ld = (3/40) × (fy / (λ√f'c)) × (ψt × ψe / cb_term) × db

With ψt = 1.3 (top bar), ψe = 1.0 (uncoated), λ = 1.0, and cb+Ktr/db = 1.5, the required development length is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Check your ψt factor (1.3 for top bars) and plug in db = 1.0 in for #8.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! ld = (3/40) × (60000/(1.0×√4000)) × (1.3×1.0/1.5) × 1.0 = 0.075 × 949 × 0.867 × 1.0 = 61.7 in. Simplified: ld ≈ 49 in using ACI table for #8 top bars in 4000 psi concrete.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect for simplified table lookup, but close to the full formula result. Check whether cb_term = 1.5 was applied.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. This exceeds the typical ld for #8 bars in 4000 psi concrete.

hint:
ACI 318 tension development length formula:
ld = (3fy)/(40λ√f'c) × (ψt ψe)/(cb+Ktr)/db × db
For top bars (ψt=1.3), uncoated (ψe=1.0), λ=1.0, f'c=4000 psi, fy=60000 psi:
Use ACI tables: #8 top bar in 4000 psi = ~49 in minimum ld
shortcut: From ACI simplified table: #8 top bar, 4000 psi → ld ≈ 49 in. Top bars always need more length (ψt = 1.3).
fifthGrader: Development length is how far a rebar must be embedded into concrete before you can trust it fully. Pull too hard on a short bar and it slides out. Top bars need extra length because the concrete below them tends to have more air bubbles, making the bond weaker.

title: Structural Detail – Shear Stirrup Spacing
description:
A beam design detail shows:

• Vu (factored shear) = 65 kips
• φVc (concrete shear strength) = 28 kips
• φ = 0.75, fyt = 60,000 psi, d = 20 in
• Stirrups: 2-leg #4 bars (Av = 2 × 0.20 = 0.40 in²)

The required stirrup spacing to carry the design shear is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Use s = (φ × Av × fyt × d) / Vs where Vs = Vu − φVc.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. Vs = Vu − φVc = 65 − 28 = 37 kips. s = (Av × fyt × d) / Vs.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. s = (0.40 × 60 × 20) / 37 = 480 / 37 = 13.0 in. Check your Vs calculation.

hint:
Step 1: Vs = Vu − φVc = 65 − 28 = 37 kips
Step 2: s = (Av × fyt × d) / Vs
Note: Use consistent units — fyt in ksi
s = (0.40 in² × 60 ksi × 20 in) / 37 kips = 480 / 37 = 13.0 in
fifthGrader: Stirrups are little U-shaped bars that hold a beam together when shear (sliding) forces try to crack it diagonally. The more shear force there is, the closer the stirrups need to be. We calculate spacing by figuring out how much shear each stirrup can handle.

title: Nomograph – Manning's Pipe Sizing Chart
description: Using a Manning's nomograph for circular pipes (n = 0.013, full flow), a pipe must carry Q = 25 cfs on a slope S = 0.005. On the nomograph, connecting Q = 25 cfs and S = 0.005 on the appropriate scales, the required pipe diameter is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Verify by direct calculation: Q = (1.486/n) × A × R^(2/3) × S^(1/2). At D=24in, Q ≈ 19.7 cfs < 25 cfs.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! From the Manning's nomograph at Q=25 cfs, S=0.005, n=0.013, the pipe diameter reads approximately 27 in. Verify: D=27in → A=3.976 ft², R=0.5625 ft, Q=(1.486/0.013)×3.976×(0.5625)^(2/3)×(0.005)^(1/2) ≈ 25 cfs ✓

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. 30 in is oversized for these flow conditions.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Significantly oversized. Re-read the nomograph at the intersection of Q and S lines.

hint:
Manning's nomograph use:
1. Locate Q = 25 cfs on the discharge scale
2. Locate S = 0.005 on the slope scale
3. Draw a straight line through both points
4. Read the diameter at the intersection with the diameter scale
Verify: D = 27 in = 2.25 ft, A = π(2.25)²/4 = 3.976 ft², R = 0.5625 ft
shortcut: At Q=25 cfs and S=0.005 with n=0.013 → nomograph reads D ≈ 27 in. Always round UP to next standard size.
fifthGrader: A nomograph is a special chart with three scales. You put a ruler across two known values and read the third where it crosses. It's a visual calculator! Here we know the flow and slope, so the chart tells us how big the pipe needs to be.

title: Hazen-Williams Chart – Pipe Friction Loss
description:
A 12-inch diameter water main (Hazen-Williams C = 140) carries Q = 1,500 gpm. Using the Hazen-Williams equation:

V = 1.318 × C × R^0.63 × S^0.54 (velocity in ft/s)

Or equivalently reading from an H-W chart, the friction loss per 1,000 ft of pipe is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. 1,500 gpm through 12-in pipe corresponds to a higher velocity. Check V = Q/A first.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Recheck: C=140 is a smooth pipe. Higher C = less friction = less head loss.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. That friction loss corresponds to a rougher pipe (lower C value).

hint:
Hazen-Williams: V = 1.318 × C × R^0.63 × S^0.54
For circular pipe: R = D/4 = 1/4 = 0.25 ft (for 12-in = 1-ft pipe)
Convert flow: 1,500 gpm ÷ 449 = 3.34 ft³/s
V = Q/A = 3.34/0.785 = 4.26 ft/s
Solve for S: S = (V/(1.318×C×R^0.63))^(1/0.54)
shortcut: Q = 1500 gpm = 3.34 cfs. V = 3.34/0.785 = 4.26 ft/s. From H-W chart at V and D → S ≈ 0.0036 → 3.6 ft/1000 ft.
fifthGrader: Water flowing through a pipe loses pressure due to friction — like trying to blow through a straw vs a garden hose. The Hazen-Williams 'C' value measures how smooth the pipe is. A smoother pipe (high C) loses less pressure per foot. We use a chart or formula to find the loss rate.

title: Culvert Nomograph – Headwater Depth
description:
A 36-inch circular concrete culvert (inlet control) carries Q = 80 cfs. Using the FHWA culvert headwater nomograph for circular pipe with a square edge entrance:

• D = 3.0 ft
• Q/D^2.5 = 80 / (3.0)^2.5 = 80 / 15.59 = 5.13

From the nomograph, at Q/D^2.5 = 5.13 with square edge entrance, the headwater ratio HW/D is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. At Q/D^2.5 = 5.13, the nomograph reads HW/D > 1.0 for a square edge entrance.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! From FHWA HDS-5 nomograph for concrete pipe, square edge entrance: at Q/D^2.5 ≈ 5.13, HW/D ≈ 1.5. HW = 1.5 × 3.0 = 4.5 ft.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. HW/D = 2.0 corresponds to higher Q/D^2.5 values.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. HW/D = 0.5 corresponds to a very small flow relative to culvert size.

hint:
FHWA Culvert Nomograph steps (inlet control):
1. Compute Q/D^2.5 = 80/(3)^2.5 = 5.13 ft^0.5/s
2. Enter nomograph on Q/D^2.5 axis
3. Read across to the appropriate entrance condition line
4. Read HW/D from the vertical axis
5. Multiply by D to get HW in feet
shortcut: Q/D^2.5 = 5.13 → from nomograph (square edge) → HW/D ≈ 1.5 → HW = 4.5 ft.
fifthGrader: A culvert is a pipe that lets water flow under a road. The headwater is how deep the water backs up behind the road before it can flow through. The nomograph lets engineers quickly read the headwater depth without doing a lot of math — they just look up the flow rate and read off the answer.

title: Moody Diagram – Friction Factor for Pipe Flow
description:
A 6-inch diameter steel pipe (absolute roughness ε = 0.00015 ft) carries water at a velocity V = 8.0 ft/s. The kinematic viscosity ν = 1.08 × 10⁻⁵ ft²/s.

The Reynolds number and the relative roughness are:
• Re = V × D / ν = 8.0 × 0.5 / (1.08×10⁻⁵) = 370,370
• ε/D = 0.00015 / 0.5 = 0.00030

Reading the Moody diagram at Re ≈ 370,000 and ε/D = 0.0003, the Darcy-Weisbach friction factor f is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. f = 0.010 is too low for this roughness and Reynolds number.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! From the Moody diagram at Re ≈ 370,000 and ε/D = 0.0003, f ≈ 0.016 (in the transitional turbulence zone). Colebrook equation confirms this.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. f = 0.020 is slightly too high. At ε/D = 0.0003 and Re = 370,000 the Moody diagram reads ≈ 0.016.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. f = 0.038 would be for a very rough pipe or laminar flow conditions.

hint:
Moody Diagram reading:
1. Compute Re = VD/ν = 8.0×0.5/(1.08×10⁻⁵) ≈ 370,000
2. Compute ε/D = 0.00015/0.5 = 0.0003
3. Find Re on x-axis, move up to ε/D = 0.0003 curve
4. Read f on y-axis ≈ 0.016
Alternative: Use Colebrook equation: 1/√f = -2 log(ε/(3.7D) + 2.51/(Re√f))
shortcut: Re = 370,000, ε/D = 0.0003 → Moody diagram → f ≈ 0.016. Fully turbulent zone begins at Re ≈ 4,000,000 for this roughness.
fifthGrader: The Moody diagram is a map for pipe friction. On one side you look up how fast the water is moving (Reynolds number). On the other you look up how rough the pipe is. Where they meet on the chart, you read the friction factor — like finding a city on a map using latitude and longitude.

title: Hydraulic Elements Chart – Velocity at Partial Depth
description:
A 30-inch circular pipe flows full at V_full = 5.0 ft/s. From the dimensionless hydraulic elements chart for circular pipes:

At d/D = 0.75 (flow depth = 22.5 inches), the velocity ratio V/V_full is approximately 1.13.

The actual flow velocity at 75% depth is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. At d/D = 0.75, the pipe does NOT flow at 75% of full velocity. Pipes can flow FASTER than full at partial depths.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. At d/D = 0.75, V/V_full = 1.13 > 1.0. The velocity exceeds full-flow velocity.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Correct! V = V/V_full × V_full = 1.13 × 5.0 = 5.65 ft/s. Circular pipes flow FASTER than full at d/D ≈ 0.80.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. V/V_full = 1.13, not 1.30. V = 1.13 × 5.0 = 5.65 ft/s.

hint:
From the hydraulic elements chart:
V/V_full at d/D = 0.75 ≈ 1.13
V_actual = (V/V_full) × V_full = 1.13 × 5.0 = 5.65 ft/s
Key fact: Maximum velocity in circular pipe occurs at d/D ≈ 0.80, where V/V_full ≈ 1.16
shortcut: V = 1.13 × 5.0 = 5.65 ft/s. Surprise: partial-full pipes can flow FASTER than full pipes!
fifthGrader: You might think a pipe with less water flows slower, but that's not always true! At about 80% full, a circular pipe actually moves water FASTER than when it's completely full. That's because the water surface creates less wall friction compared to having a full pipe touching all sides.

title: Unit Hydrograph – Peak Flow Estimation
description: A watershed has a 1-hour unit hydrograph with a peak of 450 cfs (for 1 inch of excess rainfall). A storm produces 2.5 inches of excess rainfall in 1 hour. Using linear superposition, the peak runoff from this storm is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. The unit hydrograph is for 1 inch of rainfall. Scale it by the actual rainfall depth.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. The storm produces 2.5 inches, not 2.0 inches. Q_peak = 2.5 × 450.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Correct! Q_peak = rainfall depth × unit hydrograph peak = 2.5 in × 450 cfs/in = 1,125 cfs.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Use only the excess rainfall (2.5 in), not total rainfall. Q = 2.5 × 450 = 1,125 cfs.

hint:
Unit Hydrograph Principle (linearity):
Q_peak = Excess Rainfall Depth × UH Peak Ordinate
Q = 2.5 in × 450 cfs/in = 1,125 cfs
The unit hydrograph is defined for 1 inch of EXCESS rainfall — scale linearly for other depths.
shortcut: Q = P_excess × Q_UH_peak = 2.5 × 450 = 1,125 cfs. Linear scaling is the key property of unit hydrographs.
fifthGrader: A unit hydrograph shows what a watershed does with exactly 1 inch of rain. If you get 2.5 inches instead, the flood is 2.5 times bigger — because the watershed responds proportionally. It's like scaling a recipe: if 1 egg makes 12 cookies, 2.5 eggs make 30 cookies.

title: Pipe Flow Nomograph – Velocity Check
description: A storm sewer nomograph shows that an 18-inch concrete pipe (n = 0.013) flowing full on slope S = 0.003 has a full-flow velocity of V = 4.8 ft/s. The minimum velocity for self-cleansing in a storm sewer is 3.0 ft/s. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The pipe does NOT meet minimum velocity — increase slope
options.feedback: Incorrect. V = 4.8 ft/s > 3.0 ft/s minimum. The pipe DOES meet the minimum velocity requirement.

options.label: B
options.text: The pipe meets minimum velocity — design is acceptable
options.feedback: Correct! V_full = 4.8 ft/s > V_min = 3.0 ft/s. The pipe adequately self-cleanses at full-flow conditions.

options.label: C
options.text: The pipe is too large — sediment will deposit at low flows
options.feedback: Incorrect based on full-flow data. At full flow, V = 4.8 ft/s is adequate. At partial flow, V may also be adequate (recall V_half ≈ V_full for circular pipes).

options.label: D
options.text: The velocity exceeds maximum allowable — erosion risk
options.feedback: Incorrect. 4.8 ft/s is well within normal storm sewer velocities. Maximum is typically 10-15 ft/s.

hint:
Self-cleansing velocity check:
• Storm sewers: V_min = 3.0 ft/s at design flow
• Sanitary sewers: V_min = 2.0 ft/s
• Maximum velocity (to prevent erosion): typically 10 ft/s
V_full = 4.8 ft/s > 3.0 ft/s → acceptable
shortcut: 4.8 > 3.0 ft/s minimum → OK. Storm sewer min = 3 ft/s, sanitary min = 2 ft/s. Know both!
fifthGrader: Storm sewers carry leaves, sand, and debris. If water moves too slowly, the junk settles at the bottom and clogs the pipe. Engineers set a minimum speed of 3 ft/s to make sure the pipe flushes itself clean. 4.8 ft/s is safely above that — the pipe will stay clean.

title: Flow Duration Curve – Exceedance Frequency
description:
A flow duration curve for a stream shows:

• Q at 10% exceedance = 1,200 cfs (high flows, exceeded 10% of time)
• Q at 50% exceedance = 380 cfs (median flow)
• Q at 90% exceedance = 45 cfs (low flows, exceeded 90% of time)

A water intake is designed to divert flow when Q ≥ 200 cfs. The percentage of time the intake can operate is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. At 10% exceedance, Q = 1,200 cfs. The threshold of 200 cfs falls between 50% and 90% exceedance.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. Interpolate: 200 cfs falls between 380 (50%) and 45 (90%). The exceedance is between 50% and 90%.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Correct! By linear interpolation between 50% exceedance (380 cfs) and 90% exceedance (45 cfs): % = 50 + (380−200)/(380−45) × (90−50) = 50 + (180/335)×40 = 50 + 21.5 ≈ 71.5%. Nearest answer: 65%.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. At 90% exceedance, Q = 45 cfs, which is below the 200 cfs threshold.

hint:
Flow duration curve: the curve shows what fraction of time a given flow is exceeded.
Q = 200 cfs falls between:
• 50% exceedance (Q = 380 cfs)
• 90% exceedance (Q = 45 cfs)
Interpolate: % = 50 + [(380−200)/(380−45)] × (90−50) = 50 + 21.5 = 71.5%
shortcut: Interpolate between (380 cfs, 50%) and (45 cfs, 90%): 200 cfs → ≈ 71% exceedance → intake operates ~71% of the time.
fifthGrader: A flow duration curve is like a report card for a river. It shows how often the river flows above any given level. The intake needs at least 200 cfs to work. We look at the chart to find how often the river flows that much or more.

title: NRCS TR-55 – Time of Concentration (Sheet Flow)
description:
Using the NRCS TR-55 Sheet Flow equation for time of concentration:

Tt = (0.007 × (nL)^0.8) / (P2^0.5 × s^0.4)

Where:
• n = 0.15 (dense grass)
• L = 100 ft (flow length)
• P2 = 3.6 in (2-year, 24-hr rainfall)
• s = 0.04 ft/ft (slope)

The sheet flow travel time Tt is most nearly:

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Recheck your exponent arithmetic. (nL)^0.8 ≠ nL.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. The TR-55 formula uses fractional exponents. Verify (0.15×100)^0.8 and (0.04)^0.4.

shortcut: Tt = 0.007 × 8.59 / 0.4457 = 0.135 hr. Sheet flow is the slowest travel phase — compute it first in tc.
fifthGrader: When rain falls on a grassy field, it doesn't immediately rush to a stream — it sheets across the surface slowly. This formula tells you how long it takes for that thin sheet of water to travel 100 feet. Dense grass slows it way down (high n), while steep slopes speed it up (high s).

title: IDF Chart – Reading the Correct Frequency Curve
description:
An engineer must size a storm drain for a 10-year design storm with tc = 45 minutes. The IDF chart shows the following curves from top to bottom:
100-year, 50-year, 25-year, 10-year, 5-year, 2-year FREQUENCY.

At 45-minute duration, the curves read approximately:
• 100-yr: 5.8 in/hr
• 50-yr: 5.0 in/hr
• 25-yr: 4.4 in/hr
• 10-yr: 3.7 in/hr
• 5-yr: 3.1 in/hr
• 2-yr: 2.3 in/hr

The design rainfall intensity for this storm drain is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. 3.1 in/hr is the 5-year storm. The design is for the 10-year storm.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! The 10-year frequency curve at 45-minute duration reads 3.7 in/hr. Always use the correct return period curve.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. 4.4 in/hr is the 25-year storm, not the 10-year storm.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. 5.0 in/hr is the 50-year storm. Using the wrong frequency curve is a very common PE exam error.

hint:
IDF Chart Reading — 3 Steps:
1. Identify the correct frequency curve (10-year for this problem)
2. Find the storm duration on the horizontal axis (45 minutes)
3. Read the intensity on the vertical axis at that intersection
10-year curve at 45 min → 3.7 in/hr
Common mistake: reading the wrong frequency curve!
shortcut: 10-year curve + 45 min → 3.7 in/hr. The frequency curve is labeled — count from the bottom (2-yr) up to 10-yr.
fifthGrader: An IDF chart is a family of curves, like lanes on a highway — each curve is a different storm size. The bigger the return period (50-year, 100-year), the higher the curve (more intense rainfall). You always use the curve that matches your design storm. For a 10-year drain, use the 10-year curve — not the 50-year just because it's bigger!
